newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crisis unites two Japanese communities.
newsitem.headline: Peru crisis unites two Japanese communities.

text.p: The deadlocked hostage crisis in Peru has sparked an unprecedented sense of unity between the Peruvian-Japanese community and its Japanese counterpart, members of both groups say.

"Now it's more personal," said Cesar Morisaki, a "nikkei sansei" or third-generation Peruvian of Japanese descent. "There has always been a relationship based on work and cultural events, but now we are much more united because this (incident) worries all of us."
"Our relationship has improved, and I hope this will last," agreed Luis Tamamoto, a senior official at the Peruvian-Japanese Cultural Centre.
"I strongly feel the nikkei are helping us a lot, especially when the captives are released," said Kagefumi Nagao, an official of Japanese company Ajinomoto in Lima.
The president of Ajinomoto's subsidiary in Peru is believed to be one of 74 hostages still held by Marxist rebels who stormed the residence of the Japanese ambassador on December 17.

The Peruvian-Japanese Cultural Center's 24-hour emergency commission, which works together with Japanese business groups, has won acclaim from both communities for its efficiency and the care it provides for released hostages.
"We gathered 300 volunteers in 20 minutes the day 225 captives were liberated," Luis Nohara, a senior official of the commission, told Reuters.

Despite having the same country of origin, interaction between members of the 80,000-strong nikkei community and resident Japanese nationals rarely went beyond a formal relationship before the hostage crisis.
Both sides say language barriers and cultural differences hindered intimacy between the two groups.
"We already have been here for almost four generations and unfortunately, I tell you, there are a lot who do not speak Japanese," said Nohara. "We feel well-identified with Peruvian society."
The first 790 Japanese immigrants arrived in Peru in 1899 and became farmers, though many later moved to cities to take up jobs in commerce and industry.

Peru's Japanese community, which consists of about 120 businessmen, diplomats and their families, have difficulty mastering the Spanish language and adopting Peruvian customs, since their stay in this country is mostly limited to two or three years.

Some say, however, that relations between the two communities had become closer thanks to Japanese ambassador Morihisa Aoki, host of the party stormed by Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas three weeks ago.
Toshiro Konishi, one of the hundreds of guests taken hostage, was released on December 22. He said Ambassador Aoki has organised the most events to bring the two Japanese communities together.
"Recently, he also held an Okinawan food party at his residence," said Konishi, a Japanese restaurant owner who came to Peru 22 years ago.
He added that the nikkei are sometimes more Japanese than the Japanese themselves:
"They still value 'giri-ninjo' (human sympathy and duty), which is not evident in today's Japan."

In contrast to the growing solidarity and emerging friendship of the two groups in Peru, anti-Peruvian sentiment has become evident in parts of Japan, where many Latin American nikkei work as manual labourers.

After the outbreak of the hostage crisis, some Peruvian nikkei in Isesaki, an industrial town about 65 miles (100 km) north of Tokyo, had their properties stoned and were harassed verbally by local Japanese.
Konishi, who learned about such incidents after his release, said he was very disappointed because "when we were inside, Peruvians prayed for our safety."
